#3058. ULA Vulcan Launch Ends in Disaster for Amazon's Satellite Internet Ambitions

Amazon was counting on ULA to get its Leo satellites back on track. It shouldn't have.

By Rich Smith – Nov 21, 2026 at 9:27PM EST

A crisis was forming in the space industry.

For months, Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX -7.69%) CEO Elon Musk had been making noises about ending commercial launches of its Falcon 9 rocket -- the rocket that, in 2025, launched more than 80% of all payloads to orbit worldwide. At the time, rockets from rival companies Arianespace, Blue Origin, and United Launch Alliance were all grounded for a variety of technical glitches.

Nine months ago, United Launch Alliance (ULA) suffered an anomaly with one of its Vulcan Centaur rockets, forcing it to pause operations while it worked out a fix. But at long last, ULA was ready to return to flight. In a mission slated for Nov. 15, Vulcan would return to flight, carrying a payload of 40 Leo communications satellites into orbit for customer Amazon (AMZN -4.10%).

A successful launch would advance Amazon's effort to build a satellite communications system to rival SpaceX's Starlink. At the same time, it would alleviate the concerns of space companies worried that Falcon 9's retirement would deprive them of access to space. With ULA back in the race, there'd once again be an alternative to SpaceX.

That's what a successful launch would have meant -- but it's not what actually happened.

Instead, for the first time in its history as a space company, ULA suffered a total mission failure -- all cargo lost. As ULA explained, its Vulcan rocket "lost telemetry and the mission at approximately 10 minutes into flight," although the real problem occurred before that.

Vulcan Centaur includes two stages: BE-4 engines from Blue Origin power the Vulcan first stage, supplemented by RL10 side boosters from L3Harris(LHX -2.59%). In flight, the RL10s are first to drop off the rocket, followed by the entire first stage detaching approximately six minutes into flight. Then the Centaur second stage takes over and lifts the payload the rest of the way into orbit.

After several days of examining the data, ULA now believes the RL10 boosters and the second-stage Centaur both performed nominally. The problem must therefore lie with the Vulcan first stage -- specifically, preliminary indications as of Wednesday suggest Vulcan's fuel supply to the BE-4 engines, rather than the engines themselves, was the culprit. This first stage performed poorly in the boost stage, failing to accelerate the vehicle sufficiently for the Centaur to lift the payload all the way into orbit.

For Amazon, either culprit would be bad news.

Aiming to accelerate its deployment of Leo satellites so that it can begin competing with SpaceX in satellite internet, Amazon splashed out billions of dollars to reserve launches on 38 Vulcan Centaur rockets, 18 Arianespace Ariane 6es, and anywhere from 12 to 27 Blue Origin New Glenns.

It's also reserved launches on some of ULA's older Atlas V rockets. So far, those have done most of the work of putting nearly 400 Amazon Leo satellites into orbit (with significant help from SpaceX's Falcon 9, which Amazon reluctantly added to the lineup in 2023). The problem is, ULA is just about out of Atlas V rockets (and isn't building more). And SpaceX Falcon 9 launches are all booked up through 2028 (and SpaceX also doesn't plan to add more).

This leaves Amazon largely dependent on ULA's Vulcan Centaur -- which just proved itself unreliable. And this problem may get even bigger; after all, the same BE-4 engine that appears to be at the root of Vulcan's problems also powers Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket. And that could put New Glenn on the sidelines as well.

(Or it may not. While the investigation is still at an early stage, as of Wednesday, ULA believes "preliminary indications" suggest Vulcan's fuel supply to the BE-4 engines, and not the engines themselves, is the culprit. If that's the case, then Blue Origin's New Glenn may not be affected.)

Still, until this is all resolved, it appears that Amazon currently has no reliable means of putting Leo satellites into orbit.

In the meantime, SpaceX Starlink, already the leader in satellite internet, is likely to remain so for the foreseeable future. More than that: the longer Amazon is forced to cool its heels down here on Earth, the wider the gap between SpaceX and [insert name of literally anyone else who might want to compete with SpaceX].

Amazon's pain, I fear, is going to be SpaceX's gain.

#3056. Top Wall Street analysts like these 3 dividend stocks for steady income

Stock markets remain volatile as investors weigh uncertainty in the Middle East, rising interest rates and concerns about the artificial intelligence (AI) trade.

Given this volatile backdrop, investors seeking a stable income stream can enhance their portfolios with the addition of dividend stocks. In this regard, tracking recommendations of top Wall Street analysts can help shortlist attractive dividend stocks that are backed by strong financials.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Integrated oil and gas giant Chevron (CVX) is the first dividend pick. Earlier this month, the company paid a quarterly dividend of $1.78 per share. At an annualized dividend of $7.12 per share, CVX offers a dividend yield of about 3.5%.

After a meeting with senior leadership, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on CVX and raised his price target to $240 from $225. Among the key takeaways Mehta emphasized was that Chevron is building a solid pipeline of promising international exploration projects across Latin America, the Middle East, West Africa and the Eastern Mediterranean. In particular, he mentioned the focus on Venezuela, where Chevron expects to more than double gross production to 600 kbd from about 280 kbd by 2031, using three joint ventures.

Mehta also noted Chevron's efforts to deploy new technologies, especially in shale and tight-oil operations. CVX is focused on boosting productivity and efficiency to maximize free cash flow, he added.

Initiatives such as artificial lift optimization, AI and machine learning, and advanced chemical treatments are expected to improve recovery by about 10% in new wells. Consequently, capital spending per barrel in U.S. shale is projected to fall 25% in 2026, with total Permian spending dropping below $3.5 billion.

Mehta also said that Chevron sees power as a growth opportunity and is using its U.S. natural gas portfolio, key equipment and partnerships to meet rising demand. Notably, Chevron recently signed a 20-year power purchase deal with Microsoft (MSFT) to supply 2.67 GW of behind-the-meter capacity. This project, called Kilby, is expected to see its first power delivery in 2028 and generate mid-teens returns and long-term cash flows.

Mehta ranks No. 536 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 61% of the time, delivering an average return of 11.3%. See Chevron Statistics on TipRanks.

Enterprise Products Partners (EPD) is a master limited partnership (MLP) that provides midstream energy services to producers and consumers of natural gas, natural gas liquids (NGLs), crude oil, refined products and petrochemicals. With a quarterly cash distribution of 56 cents per common unit ($2.24 per common unit annualized), EPD offers a yield of about 6%.

Following a recent call with the company, RBC Capital analyst Elvira Scotto reiterated a buy rating on EPD with a price target of $42. The analyst slightly lowered her estimates for the second half of 2026, citing margin and volume normalization, though demand dynamics remain strong.

While the 5-star analyst expects a sequential decline due to normal seasonality and normalization following high spreads in the first half of the year, she still expects EPD to report another solid quarter (Q3 2026) and enter 2027 with a favorable setup. Ahead of Q3 earnings, Scotto expects investors to focus on export demand durability, EPD's ability to profit from spot cargo sales and growth in Permian volumes.

Scotto continues to expect $150 million of common unit buybacks per quarter in the second half of 2026. She expects buybacks to increase to $200 million per quarter in 2027, as capex spending declines and free cash flow improves.

In total, Scotto is bullish on EPD and views it as a core MLP holding that has both offensive and defensive characteristics. The analyst praised EPD's diverse asset base as ensuring stable cash flows. "Furthermore, the partnership's multi-year organic growth backlog helps provide visibility on long-term distribution growth," Scotto said.

Scotto ranks No. 199 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been successful 67% of the time, delivering an average return of 15.9%. See Enterprise Products Partners Financials on TipRanks.

Brookfield Infrastructure Partners (BIP) operates a diversified portfolio of high-quality utilities, transport, midstream and data assets. The company declared a quarterly distribution of 45.5 cents per unit, payable on September 29. At an annualized distribution of $1.82, BIP offers a yield of 5.2%.

"Layering in the benefits from the proposed corporate simplification, a multiple well below historical levels and an attractive yield, we believe BIP offers a compelling risk/reward and it remains a preferred idea," said Dodge.

With more organic growth projects in the pipeline and new partnership investment opportunities, Dodge believes that BIP has clearer visibility into where it will deploy capital. That should support continued double-digit growth in funds from operations (FFO) per unit.

Dodge said the semiconductor foundries that BIP is developing with Intel (INTC) are expected to be fully commissioned by the end of 2026, with returns improving through Q4 2026. Dodge expects the joint venture to boost FFO by 300-400 basis points.

Scholarships vary in what they pay for and who can apply. Understanding the differences can save you time during your application process.

Scholarships have become a standard part of applying for college. You can learn about scholarships in a variety of ways, but looking through an online database of available scholarships — the most common way — can be overwhelming.

Before you go searching for a scholarship, it's important to understand the types of scholarships available and how to identify the ones that give you the best chance of winning, which can save you time and potentially earn you more funding. Here’s what you need to know about scholarships to decide which ones are best for you.

Scholarships are often funded by three groups: private organizations, institutions like universities, and government agencies. None is better than the other when it comes to awarding funds.

Nonprofit organizations and clubs that are looking for students either majoring in or researching certain fields, or who have experience volunteering in a specific field.

Companies that want to support all students or only fund those majoring in a field that relates to the companies’ industries.

Financial institutions, such as banks or credit unions, that want to support their community or their members.

Individuals or families that are funding private scholarships, usually in memory of a loved one.

Universities and colleges that are offering funds to students who attend their campuses.

Research organizations that want to fund students who will research in their areas of interest and further their causes.

These scholarships generally are provided by local, state or federal government agencies for a variety of reasons. Despite being funded by a government agency, the scholarships do not require you to pay back the money — unlike federal student loans.

Some scholarships pay for anything related to college expenses, including tuition, room and board, books and supplies, and more. Other scholarships limit what you can pay for with the funds, such as only tuition or tuition along with books. It’s important to look at this restriction when applying for scholarships to ensure the funds will go toward what you need to cover.

Merit scholarships require you to show excellence or achievements in your schoolwork, through talents and abilities, and even leadership or service work. Because these types of awards can be highly competitive, merit scholarships might require more than just achievements, such as volunteer or leadership experience. This means merit-based scholarships can overlap with other types of scholarship categories. Here are some examples of merit-based scholarships:

Merit scholarships often require you to have earned a minimum grade point average (GPA). The minimum GPA depends on the scholarship but often ranges from 2.0 to 4.0, with more competitive scholarships usually requiring higher GPAs. Scholarships with lower GPA minimums are more likely to consider additional factors, such as financial need.

Some merit scholarships might require a minimum ACT or SAT score instead of a GPA — or in addition to a minimum GPA.

Merit scholarships might also require applicants to have participated in activities outside of their schoolwork. This is common for scholarships that require membership in a certain group or organization. For example, membership in agricultural clubs, such as 4-H or FFA, and scouting groups, such as the National Eagle Scout Association, appear in scholarship requirements.

Some scholarships emphasize volunteering or community service and only consider applicants who have that experience. Applications vary in how detailed their requirements can be. Some scholarships want only a general description of where and how you’ve volunteered, and others might require experience with a service project that shows more leadership experience or time volunteering with a certain type of organization.

Scholarships that are awarded to students who can’t afford college are called need-based scholarships.

Unmet financial need is the difference between what it will cost you to attend college and what you can afford to pay. Because calculating how much you can afford is a complicated process, many scholarships refer to your FAFSA to document your financial need.

Some scholarship requirements may be as straightforward as demonstrating that you have financial need, but some scholarships might have income limits. However, income restrictions are less common.

Athletic scholarships are for — you guessed it — athletes. They are usually offered by colleges and universities to recruit athletes onto their collegiate teams and can be competitive. Which sports have scholarships available and the scholarship amounts vary by college.

Even though the main criterion for an athletic scholarship is being good at your sport, you’ll likely still need to show that you can keep up with your schoolwork. Most athletic scholarships require students to earn a minimum GPA or test scores to remain eligible while they’re in college.

Some scholarships are designated for students majoring in a general field, such as science or education, but others can be for very specific areas of study. For example, a scholarship for students majoring in a natural resource field could include majors in biology, ecology, wildlife biology, conservation education, forestry, soils and hydrology. However, a stricter scholarship might state that students have to major in more specific topics, such as biochemistry or microbial ecology.

Scholarships are available for active and former members of the military and members of their families. In addition to federal funds available for veterans to attend college, private organizations and some universities have scholarships for veterans to offset the cost of a degree.

Which family members can apply for funds depends on the individual scholarship. For example, some scholarships extend to children or spouses of veterans, but some go as far in a family tree as great-grandchildren.

Veteran- and military-focused scholarships might require that applicants or their family members enlisted in a certain branch, served during a particular time or conflict, or meet a certain rank or status such as receiving disability. Scholarships might also require that the applicant be a wartime veteran or family member of a wartime veteran; not all veterans meet this status.

Scholarships are also awarded to people who identify with a certain group. Common examples of identity-based scholarships include those for people who have disabilities, belong to certain ethnic or religious groups, identify as LGBTQIA+ or are first-generation students. Some identity-based scholarships require applicants to meet several criteria, such as belonging to more than one identity group.

Outside of what would be considered standard DEI groups, there are scholarships for applicants who identify with less common groups, such as veganism, homelessness and model railroad builders.

The best scholarships for you depend on your situation. For example, if you are a skilled athlete with a good academic record, going for an athletic scholarship might give you the most funding. On the other hand, if you’re going to research a topic that isn’t common, looking for scholarships that support your research topic might be your best bet because competition could be lower.

Good tactics to figure out which scholarships are worth your time include:

Think of the skills, talents, experience and identities that are unique to you. For example, being a child of a veteran immediately qualifies you for scholarships with fewer applicants than scholarships open to everyone. Likewise, if you embrace a certain ethnicity, identify with a specific group or have experience with a type of work, you might qualify for scholarships that appreciate and recognize those attributes more than the average scholarship.

Apply if you think you're eligible. Don’t apply to just a few scholarships and hope you get them. Instead, apply for as many scholarships as you can and for which you’re eligible. This increases your chances of receiving funds. Even small scholarships can make a big impact when you add several of them together.

Understand how you can use the money. If you already have a scholarship that covers only books, applying for the same type of scholarship isn’t helpful if you don’t need the extra funds. Instead, look for scholarships that cover the costs you have remaining.

Not sure where to look? Our sister site Scholarships360.org provides students with vetted scholarship opportunities. That would be a good place to start.

#3051. SunPower: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Virtual power plants carry a higher contribution margin than traditional third-party ownership, which matters more as residential demand weakens.

By The Motley Fool Team – Nov 21, 2026 at 9:40PM EST

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 19, 2026, SunPower (SPWR -31.84%) outlined a corporate turnaround strategy focused on commercial growth, virtual power plant systems, and cost reduction. The end of the residential solar tax credit hit retail installation volumes, forcing management to pivot toward higher-margin commercial contracts and operational efficiency to stem losses. Three things management said on the call stand out.

Commercial installations generate higher gross profit per project than residential systems, averaging $330,000 per job compared to under $50,000 for standard home setups. Expanding commercial sales across 10 distinct market segments helps diversify revenue as traditional residential solar demand slows.

Virtual power plant (VPP: networked battery systems that sell excess electricity to the grid during peak pricing hours) installations yield superior profitability compared to traditional solar deployments. Building larger battery capacities creates electricity arbitrage opportunities, generating higher margins than standard third-party ownership (TPO: financing contracts where an outside entity owns the residential equipment) sales.

Management executed a reduction in force (RIF: a planned, permanent elimination of job positions) to lower operating expenses following operational integration delays and legacy overhead. Lowering headcount aligns cost structures with current shipment volumes while the company works to eliminate non-cash accounts receivable (AR: unpaid customer invoices) write-offs.

Long-term power market trends continue to favor solar adoption as utility electricity costs increase, and management is not hiding its focus on expanding high-margin sales channels.

The company relies on pre-assembled roof installation kits and exclusive supply agreements for high-efficiency solar modules to protect project margins. Management is watching conversion rates on its work-in-process (WIP: active jobs moving through assembly), state-level expansion, and positive operating cash flow within two quarters.

Growth now hinges on scaling commercial contracts and expanding virtual power plant deployments across new geographic markets to surpass baseline residential revenue.

#3048. Billionaire David Tepper Just Made a Massive AI Chip Rotation — Will It Pay Off?

Tepper was selling shares of AMD, Broadcom, and Alphabet in Q3, while buying Nvidia and Micron.

By Geoffrey Seiler – Nov 21, 2026 at 10:00PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Advanced Micro Devices ›

David Tepper of Appaloosa Management is considered one of the world's top hedge fund managers, and through his investment prowess, he's amassed an estimated net worth of $28.5 billion. The Carolina Panthers' owner was reshuffling his artificial intelligence (AI) semiconductor positions in Q3, exiting positions in Advanced Micro Devices (AMD -13.25%) and Broadcom (AVGO -12.19%), while buying shares of Nvidia (NVDA -14.01%) and Micron (MU -13.89%). He also cut his stake in Alphabet (GOOGL -2.70%) (GOOG -2.59%) nearly in half.

While Tepper's track record speaks for itself, I think he got it wrong in this case. Here's why.

While Tepper was buying Nvidia shares before Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO, the company is facing potential issues beyond the loss of its CEO. Competitors have started to catch up, with Semianalysis recently reporting that Alphabet's Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), which it co-developed with Broadcom, are delivering better performance per dollar. Meanwhile, all of Nvidia's largest customers, outside of Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX -7.69%) are working on developing their own custom chips.

The AI application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) market is growing much more quickly than the GPU market, with Counterpoint Research projecting that custom AI chip unit shipments will surpass data center GPU shipments in 2028. Two of the biggest winners from this trend are Alphabet and Broadcom.

Alphabet developed its TPUs more than a decade ago, and its comprehensive ecosystem is starting to rival Nvidia's. Not only is TPU growth supported by Alphabet's internal use and its cloud offering, but it is also beginning to sell its solutions to external data center operators, such as Anthropic and OpenAI.

Bloomberg Intelligence believes that TPU sales outside of Google Cloud could grow from just $12 billion this year to over $135 billion in 2028. This is a huge revenue driver for both Alphabet and Broadcom, which appear to be two of the biggest winners in this rotation.

Even bigger news for Nvidia competitors, though, is that Anthropic (ANT -8.50%) revealed that its Claude Mythos model demonstrated that it can get models up to speed running on AMD GPUs in just two to three days without any human involvement, dramatically cutting down the six to 12 months it used to take a dozen engineers to get models running on different chips. This greatly narrows Nvidia's CUDA moat and opens the door for both AMD and ASICs to take market share.

The timing is great for AMD, as it recently started shipping its complete Helios systems, which combine its GPUs, CPUs, and networking into one package, to large hyperscaler customers. It's significantly cheaper than Nvidia's end-to-end server racks, opening the door to take more market share if it can show strong performance. The company's CPUs will also play a key role in Alphabet's new TPU 8tx AI system.

With CUDA's moat weakening, Alphabet, Broadcom, and AMD, all of which have cheaper offerings, should benefit greatly in the coming years. Meanwhile, Nvidia could face not just a loss of share but also margin compression. This could lead to lower profitability even if it can grow its revenue. That's one of the big reasons I prefer the three stocks Tepper was selling over Nvidia.

As for the other semiconductor stock that Tepper was buying, Micron, I'd be careful. Memory has historically experienced very big boom-and-bust cycles, and, while this supercycle is certainly different, memory still tends to be a commodity.

Micron is also the most exposed of the big dynamic random access memory (DRAM) makers to any changes in prices of conventional memory, with it having the smallest share of the high bandwidth memory (HBM) market, which has been the driving force of the industry.

Another area of worry is with NAND, or flash memory. While Micron derives the bulk of its memory from DRAM, NAND has grown to about a quarter of its revenue. Hong Kong-based GF Securities recently issued a note saying it expects this market to become oversupplied as soon as next year. While primarily a DRAM maker, Micron would not be immune to a big price pullback in the NAND market.

#3043. 3 Industrial Stocks Trading Above $500 a Share: Which One Splits First?

Caterpillar, Comfort Systems, and GE Vernova all have very high stock prices that a stock split would help address.

By Reuben Gregg Brewer – Nov 21, 2026 at 10:10PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Caterpillar ›

Wall Street gets excited about stock splits, with some investors attempting to get ahead of a split before it is announced. Caterpillar (CAT -5.01%), Comfort Systems (FIX -6.42%), and GE Vernova (GEV -7.53%) are all candidates for a stock split, with share prices that are, in some cases, well above $500. Even after the pullback in the artificial intelligence trade, each of these stocks remains a strong candidate for a stock split. Based on its price, Comfort Systems could be the first to do so. Here's what you need to know.

From a purely functional point of view, a stock split makes a company's stock cheaper. For example, as of this writing, Comfort Systems' stock price was roughly $1,100 per share (rounding down). A two-for-one split would lower that to around $550 per share; a 10-for-1 split would bring the price down to $110. It is clearly easier for an investor to afford to buy a single share of a $110 stock than it is to buy a single share of a $1,100 stock. That's as true on the financial side as it is one the emotional side, since buying a single share may not feel worth the effort while buying 10 feels like a more substantial investment, even if both investments would end up costing $1,100.

From a financial perspective, however, a stock split has very little meaning. All that is being done is that a single share is now split into two or some other number of shares. To keep the math simple, if a company had just one share, it would represent 100% ownership. A two-for-one split would simply mean that there were two shares, each representing 50% ownership. A 10-for-1 split would mean there were 10 shares, each representing 10% ownership. If you owned the original share, representing 100% ownership, you would own more shares and still have 100% ownership after a stock split. Nothing changed about the percentage of the company you own.

Meanwhile, per-share figures such as earnings per share are adjusted, but the base number remains the same. For example, if a company with one share earned $10, earnings per share would be $10. After a 10-for-1 split, the company's earnings per share would be $1, but its earnings would still be $10. Again, nothing material changed about the company.

In other words, a stock split isn't a particularly big deal. But investors often view such events as important and bid up the shares of companies that split their stocks. That remains true even as more brokers allow fractional purchases, which means you can invest a dollar amount rather than buy based on the number of whole shares you can afford.

Right now, the stock prices of each of these companies are falling. That reduces the likelihood of a cut, with GE Vernova and Comfort Systems both off their 52-week highs by nearly 50%, and Caterpillar down roughly 35% from its high. Stock splits often happen on the way up; they are less likely on the way down. The pullback is due to investors being less enthusiastic about the artificial intelligence (AI) trade than earlier in the year.

Caterpillar makes construction equipment for building AI data centers and the power systems that supply them. GE Vernova makes turbines that generate the energy AI needs to operate, with demand coming from utilities and, increasingly, directly from data center operators looking to generate their own power. And Comfort Systems is a building and service provider that works on mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems, all of which are important for building an AI data center.

All three of these industrial companies have huge backlogs and will likely benefit from AI spending for years to come. That said, Comfort Systems has the highest stock price here, at a bit over $1,100. Cat is next at around $750, with GE Vernova at a bit over $530. And that's after the large drawdowns noted above. Given this information, Comfort Systems seems like the most likely candidate for a stock split.

At the end of the day, stock splits are more of an emotional phenomenon than a financial one. You probably shouldn't buy a stock just because you think it may split. You should buy it because you like the company enough to own it, preferably for the long term.

#3042. Top Wall Street analysts are upbeat about the prospects for these 3 stocks

September ended on a mixed note, with the S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average falling 0.5% and 4.3%, respectively, while the Nasdaq Composite climbed 1.9%. Markets remained on edge with higher oil prices and Treasury yields weighing on investor sentiment and triggering fears of additional interest rate hikes.

In this climate, investors with a long-term horizon can track recommendations from top Wall Street analysts to find stocks with solid growth prospects.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Neocloud company CoreWeave (CRWV) is benefiting from robust AI-driven demand for cloud computing.

Recently, JPMorgan analyst Samik Chatterjee upgraded CoreWeave to buy from hold, raising his price target to $125 from $120. The analyst cited favorable pricing, driven by solid demand, for the upgrade.

Chatterjee said CoreWeave is now more willing to sign premium priced, shorter-term contracts, which lift his revenue and margin estimates. CRWV stock performance has been underwhelming as investors worry about high capital spending, the analyst noted. That said, he believes that higher prices and increased margins will more than offset the rise in debt to fund capital spending, improving the stock's valuation.

Chatterjee noted the 25% price hike in July across CoreWeave's product offerings and frequent price increases by rivals like Nebius (NBIS), adding that some peers are charging nearly three times more for short-term compute contracts than what CoreWeave charges on longer-term deals.

"CoreWeave's leverage of the opportunity [is] evident in its recent press release highlighting contracts signed in F3Q at ~$40M/MW," said Chatterjee. JPMorgan said higher pricing is already contributing 5-10 percentage points to contract margins versus earlier deals.

Chatterjee ranks No. 4 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 75% of the time, delivering an average return of 55.3%. See CoreWeave Statistics on TipRanks.

Palo Alto Networks (PANW) is a provider of cybersecurity solutions across network, cloud, security operations, AI and identity. Following a discussion with management, BTIG analyst Gray Powell reiterated a buy rating on PANW and raised his price target to $425 from $404.

After a review of Palo Alto's product-level growth catalysts, Powell sees clear upside to both revenue and next-generation security (NGS) annual recurring revenue (ARR) in fiscal 2027. He expects PANW to deliver pro forma revenue growth of more than 17%, above the consensus estimate of 14.6%, and NGS ARR growth of more than 26% versus the Street's expectation of 24.5%.

Over the past five years, the Palo Alto business mix, has moved to higher-growth product areas and new markets. from what was earlier viewed as a hardware-centric network security company, Powell said. The 5-star analyst estimates that hardware firewalls and attached subscriptions now account for less than 50% of revenue.

Meanwhile, high-growth solutions, including Prisma SASE, software firewalls, Cortex XSIAM, Chronosphere and Idira now represent more than 35% of PANW's revenue. "Investors may not fully realize the growth potential within PANW's platform story," Powell said.

BTIG is optimistic about the prospects of Chronosphere in observability, CyberArk in identity and software firewalls and Prisma AIRS in the network and AI security business.

Powell ranks No. 320 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 61% of the time, delivering an average return of 17.3%. See Palo Alto Networks KPIs on TipRanks.

In a research note on September 30, Rosenblatt analyst Scott Devitt reiterated a buy rating on e-commerce and cloud computing platform Amazon (AMZN), raising his price target to $360 from $335. Fears that agentic commerce poses a major threat to Amazon's advertising business seem "overstated," he said.

Devitt noted that the growing adoption of personal agents and AI shopping assistants has sparked concern about displacement of Amazon's retail media business. But the 5-star analyst remains bullish, given Amazon's ability to adapt to changing consumer behavior, as it's done in the past.

Additionally, Devitt argues that even if an AI agent helps a shopper discover a product, Amazon can still handle the purchase and delivery, keeping much of the transaction value. He highlighted that management believes that existing Amazon shoppers will likely continue to start their shopping journey on the platform because it has better personalization, accurate pricing and inventory information that third-party agents still lack.

Overall, Devitt expects Amazon's retail business to prove a net beneficiary of agentic commerce. Fewer clicks would not hurt the company if the value of each remaining click and overall volumes keep rising, he said. The argument is that even if Amazon loses some sponsored ad revenue over the next few years, it would likely be only a small part of the company's total business and could be offset by growth in other areas.

"Consistent with our AI framework, we continue to view Amazon as one of the most resilient leaders in our coverage, combining owned compute infrastructure with a physical fulfillment moat," said Devitt. His bullish view is supported, Devitt said, by expectations that Amazon Web Services (AWS) will exit the year at a more than 45% growth rate with continued margin improvement.

Devitt ranks No. 765 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 49% of the time, delivering an average return of 12%. See Amazon Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

#3037. Midterms 2026: Here's Exactly What I'm Doing With My Investment Portfolio Right Now

Investors don’t need to do a lot of post-election portfolio tinkering, but some ETFs may be worth examining.

By Todd Shriber – Nov 21, 2026 at 10:30PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Vanguard Energy ETF ›

Elections have a way of eliciting emotional, borderline-visceral reactions in the investment community. Still, the knee-jerk responses are often confined to the immediate aftermath and, over time, cooler heads ultimately prevail.

For those in the camp of doing nothing with their portfolios following the blue wave, there's nothing wrong with that line of thinking. That's a calm, rational approach, and one that is validated by history.

Since 1950, the S&P 500 (^GSPC -3.70%) has been positive in the year following every midterm election, with an average gain of 15% over those 12 months. So if history holds up, now isn't the time to sell stocks.

Investors don’t need to do a lot post-election portfolio tinkering, but these ETFs may be worth examining. Image source: Getty Images.

On the other hand, changes in congressional majorities may usher in opportunities for tactical investors to capitalize on the new legislative landscape. Likewise (and perhaps surprisingly), some sectors and industries previously considered vulnerable to the Democratic sweep may prove to be less so. With that in mind, here are some exchange-traded funds (ETFs) I'm spying following the election.

It's not surprising that the healthcare sector is in the spotlight following Election Day, but this is an example of investors needing to be tactical. Said another way, a standard pharmaceutical-heavy ETF may not be the best way to capitalize on the shift of power in Congress. That's why I'm evaluating the iShares U.S. Healthcare Providers ETF (IHF +0.74%).

This $1.6 billion ETF, which turned 20 years old in May, holds shares of health insurance providers and service operators. Those could be some of the best healthcare stocks to own at a time when Democrats could push to restore, even in part, the Affordable Care Act's enhanced premium subsidies that fell by the wayside at the end of 2025. There's also chatter about momentum to add long-term care coverage to Medicare, which could benefit some of this ETF's 61 holdings.

The new congressional majority could also scrap or significantly limit planned cuts to Medicaid. If Democrats are successful in leveraging government funding to increase insurance coverage, some of this ETF's holdings will benefit from higher enrollment and reduced exposure to uncompensated care.

Be advised that this ETF is top-heavy, as UnitedHealth and CVS Health combine for nearly a third of its portfolio.

The Vanguard Energy ETF (VDE -0.73%) and the Vanguard Information Technology ETF (VGT -7.00%) are both examples of sector ETFs that were decked following Election Day. Since Nov. 4, the first trading day after Election Day, the energy fund dipped 5.3% while its tech counterpart slumped 15.3%.

The reasons differ. As has been widely noted, data center stocks are retreating not only because Democrats will control Congress but also because the party holds 30 of 50 governors' mansions, including some in states where data centers were front and center on Election Day.

Clearly, rhetoric opposed to data centers is effective on the campaign trail. Still, the Vanguard tech ETF may not be worth dumping today because it's hard to get data center moratoriums across the legislative finish line. Before Election Day, only New York state was successful in climbing that mountain.

As for the Vanguard Energy ETF, its post-election weakness isn't surprising. Renewable energy stocks often rally when polls and election results favor Democrats while the fossil fuel names that dominate this Vanguard ETF languish. That scenario played out this year.

Don't rush to abandon or ignore this Vanguard fund. The reasoning is simple: The energy sector has noteworthy short-term earnings momentum, and the group is proving to be an effective portfolio hedge while high interest rates diminish the diversification benefits of bonds.

On that note, it should be acknowledged that energy stocks have been negatively correlated with the broader market for much of this year, implying that the Vanguard Energy ETF can enhance a portfolio’s diversification.

#3030. Netflix Falls Below $60. Bill Ackman Explains Why That’s an Incredible Investment Opportunity.

A lower share price in the short term could be great in the long run.

By Adam Levy – Nov 21, 2026 at 11:00PM EST

Netflix's (NFLX -2.96%) share price has been cut in half from the all-time high it reached last summer. The stock now trades below $60 per share, as of this writing.

While there are reasons for the huge drop in Netflix, including slowing revenue growth and concerns about engagement, the drop prompted billionaire investor Bill Ackman to add the stock back to Pershing Square's (PS -8.77%) portfolio earlier this year. The stock has continued to drop, though, but Ackman doesn't see that as a concern. In fact, he sees it as an incredible opportunity for investors.

To be sure, Netflix's revenue growth has slowed considerably this year. Revenue grew between 15.9% and 17.6% in the four quarters through the first quarter of this year. That rate slowed to 13.4% in the second quarter and 11.8% in the third quarter. Management forecasts just 11.5% growth in the fourth quarter.

Management wasn't afraid to touch on the reasons for the slowdown. Co-CEO Ted Sarandos said the U.S. is "just not growing as fast as it could or as fast as we'd like," during the company's third-quarter earnings call. The advertising business has also been weaker than expected. "We are currently a bit behind our aggressive target for the year," Co-CEO Greg Peters said on the call. And that stems from disappointing engagement. "We want to grow view hours faster. We're not satisfied. We're working on it," CFO Spencer Neumann said.

But investors may be overlooking a key detail about Netflix's business that hasn't changed even as revenue growth slows. Management is highly effective at dialing in content spend and reaching its target operating margin. Operating margin is on track to reach 31.5% this year, up from 29.5% last year.

What's more, Netflix's free cash flow conversion is very high and growing. It generated $9.5 billion of free cash flow through the first three quarters of the year. Netflix uses that cash to buy back shares, which supports significant improvements in its earnings per share.

That's where Ackman believes the current share price makes Netflix stock a compelling buy. "We'll make more money over time if the stock is cheaper in the short- to intermediate-term because they're going to cancel a lot more shares as a result," he said in a recent interview.

Netflix repurchased $4.8 billion of its stock in the third quarter, and it still has $22.3 billion in authorization capacity. At the company's current share price, the remaining authorization represents around 9% of the current share count.

Netflix could complete the remaining authorization over the next two years. Management expects to generate about $2.5 billion in free cash flow in the fourth quarter, and that number should steadily climb next year. The company should be able to maintain its double-digit revenue growth rate for the foreseeable future with improvements in advertising, pricing, and maintaining a low churn rate while operating margin continues to expand. That should result in higher free cash flow conversion, meaning free cash flow grows even faster than earnings.

Ackman and his team project earnings-per-share growth of 19% per year over the next three to five years, driven by Netflix's share repurchase program. The market is pricing Netflix shares at just 22 times its free cash flow, and considering that cash is going right back to shareholders through buybacks, it seems like a fantastic opportunity for investors.

#3025. Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta Platforms Is Pouring Up to $145 Billion Into AI This Year. Investors Should Watch This 1 Number.

By Neil Patel – Nov 21, 2026 at 11:11PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Meta Platforms ›

Mark Zuckerberg founded Facebook in his Harvard dorm room in 2004. It didn't take long to grow the social media platform into one of the most powerful technology enterprises on Earth. Called Meta Platforms (META -5.93%) today, it sports a market capitalization of $1.6 trillion.

That sort of value creation should force investors to always give Zuckerberg free rein over his vision and how he directs the company's financial resources and talent. This is true even though recent blunders, like the metaverse project, haven't panned out. The ”Magnificent Seven” stock is up more than 1,500% since the initial public offering (as of Nov. 17), so his actions have clearly benefited shareholders.

It's much harder now to believe that Zuckerberg is following the right strategic path. Meta will invest up to $145 billion in capital expenditures (capex) in 2026, with spending likely to be much higher next year. This has turned free cash flow negative and led to a pause in share buybacks.

In Zuckerberg's mind, it's all about artificial intelligence (AI). Nervous investors need to watch this one number to judge if all this capex is actually worth it.

Meta's entire business model rests on monetizing the attention of people who interact with its free social media services. It currently has 3.64 billion daily active users across its family of apps, a gigantic figure that somehow keeps growing. The company makes its money from advertising, which represented 98% of total revenue in Q3 2026.

The logical conclusion is that Meta's AI-related spending spree is the right move if it improves advertising metrics. So far, this appears to be the case. This is already a huge business, but the growth has been fantastic.

Ad revenue rose 25.9% year over year to $63.1 billion in the third quarter. This is just slightly below what Alphabet's (GOOGL -2.70%) (GOOG -2.59%) Google Search, which is growing at a much slower pace, generated in Q3. Digging deeper, Meta's average price per ad increased 14%, and impressions were up 10%.

The ad ecosystem operates like a flywheel, benefiting from a robust network effect. Improving algorithms drive higher user engagement. Data is collected on their interests. Consequently, this attracts advertisers that want to get in front of these people. Meta generates revenue that is reinvested into its technology stack, further reinforcing the feedback loop.

AI appears to be strengthening the overall ad ecosystem. On the engagement front, advanced AI models bolster content recommendation. For advertisers, Meta is "leveraging AI to make it easier for businesses to manage campaigns, develop creative, and act on performance opportunities," according to chief financial officer Susan Li.

The company has developed and launched other AI-related offerings. It sells AI tools to small businesses and enterprises. There is insatiable demand for excess compute, which Meta previously said it can sell at premium prices to outside customers. The popular Muse personal agent can bring in subscription sales and capture commerce revenue share as well. These are immaterial right now, however.

Advertising is the most important area that investors should watch closely. It's a signal that the hundreds of billions of dollars in capex is driving better financial performance in the core operations. And perhaps most importantly, a thriving ad segment suggests Meta's economic moat is widening.

The AI infrastructure providers get all the love from Wall Street. This includes the chipmakers, cloud platforms, and AI model developers. Their trillion-dollar valuations reflect the market's appreciation.

But maybe the ultimate winners won't be the companies creating AI. That's an idea worth considering. Most of the value could eventually accrue to businesses that leverage this impressive technology to better serve their customers and improve their lives in unique ways.

Based on how well its ad machine is working, Meta is doing exactly this.

#3022. Junk bonds are 'flashing yellow.' Watch these warning signs

Cracks are forming in the junk bond market as investors demand higher payouts for owning the market's riskiest debt. It isn't time to ditch high-yield bonds, but investors should pay attention to the warning signs.

High-yield bonds now yield 8.1%, up from 7.22% a month ago. The increase reflects a jump in yields across the curve as investors bake in more inflation from high energy prices and other pressures, including concern about the deficit — hitting nearly $2 trillion in the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30.

The high-yield market is also showing stress on the credit side with spreads recently widening to levels not seen since April, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. Credit spreads are the difference in yield between the bonds and Treasurys of similar maturities. Wider spreads mean investors are demanding higher yields for holding corporate debt, viewing it as riskier.

Spreads are at 315 basis points in the overall high-yield market, higher than a year ago but still below levels in March when they reached 346 bps. One basis point equals one one-hundredth of a percent, or 0.01%.

The high-yield market consists of bonds rated BB+ by S&P and Fitch and Ba1 and under by Moody's. The lowest-rated cohort, CCC and below, has seen the most movement with spreads climbing dramatically over the past year to roughly 1,250 bps.

Right now, the high-yield market is "flashing yellow" but is "far from red," said Michael Arone, chief investment strategist at State Street Investment Management.

It makes sense that investors are demanding more compensation for taking on additional credit risk as borrowing costs rise, he said.

Yields are elevated across the board with the 10-year Treasury reaching its highest level since 2002 earlier in the week.

"The bigger question is whether this is simply a repricing of interest rate risk, or the beginning of a more fundamental reassessment of credit quality," Arone said.

He's in a wait-and-see mode since earnings are still growing, interest-coverage ratios remain good, and while default rates have ticked up some, he believes it is not concerning.

That said, the starting point in spreads is likely weighing on investors' psyche, since they are still low by historical standards.

"There's a small margin of error here, which I also think raises the anxiety level," Arone explained. "The compensation that investors are receiving for taking on this credit risk isn't overwhelming relative to history, and therefore subtle changes in credit spreads can be concerning."

While there may be concerns about part of the lower-rated market, the overall high-yield market is in good fundamental shape.

In fact, credit quality is at a record high, with BB bonds making up over 60% of the market compared with 38% prior to the global financial crisis, said Kelley Gerrity, a fixed income strategist at Morgan Stanley Investment Management.

"We've had higher-quality companies coming in, and with higher rates now, you also have more discipline from companies that are more indebted ... just because of the higher cost of capital, so that actually is creating a bit of a healthier picture as well," she said.

The lowest tier of high yield has always been more speculative, since the bonds have a higher default risk. Therefore, it's no surprise that they are the ones seeing the most widening in spreads, said Collin Martin, head of fixed income research and strategy at the Schwab Center for Financial Research.

The overall move in high-yield spreads have been "orderly," he said. "Are there cracks forming? I think the cracks are logical cracks with the lowest-rated bonds and it's too early to say that it's spreading to the broad credit market."

In addition, fluctuations within the CCC-rated and lower spreads have been idiosyncratic, Gerrity added. Morgan Stanley recently broke down the spreads in the lowest cohort into two buckets: performing assets and non-performing assets, which are defined as spreads above 1,000 bps.

The non-performing spread to worst is 2,818 bps, while the performing bucket — the biggest piece of the CCC market — is 461 bps, she said.

"It is isolated," she said. "I'm not necessarily sure that that will go away anytime soon, but it doesn't tell the story of overall concern and flashing caution for credit markets right now."

For now, investors should remain selective within higher yield, Gerrity advised.

"We're looking for the best relative value opportunities, and we think that exists within that single-B cohort, and so we're leaning into that," she said.

Investors should be concerned if there is a steep widening in the broader high-yield market.

But there's scant evidence of stress in the BB cohort. Spreads in that group are at 194 bps, up from 179 bps a year ago — although the move hasn't been in a straight line.

"We're going to be focusing our attention on what are considered some stronger businesses," Martin said. "If we start to see the markets demand higher spreads there also, that's what we'll be looking at to see if risks are really rising."

It's also important to understand that the Federal Reserve is raising rates in a strong economic environment, said R.J. Gallo, chief investment officer of global fixed income at Federated Hermes. The central bank is concerned about an inflation problem amid high fossil fuel prices due to the Iran war, while growth has been stronger than expected, he noted.

"With growth being good as the reason that the Fed is hiking, then you wouldn't expect high yield to blow out because growth means revenues stay up, means cash flow and profitability stays up," he explained.

High yield becomes a disaster when the economy is heading into a sharp economic downturn, Gallo said.

"That's when spreads really widen out," he said. "But a recession is not the odds-on bet. Now, talk to me in six months if the Fed keeps hiking over and over, if oil prices stay high for longer, well, then maybe we will start to wonder."

#3018. SharonAI: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Its secured-debt funding model means every GPU is backed by a customer contract, so the cash-flow test is whether those contracts convert to billing.

By The Motley Fool Team – Nov 21, 2026 at 11:14PM EST

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 16, 2026, SharonAI (SHAZ -18.06%) introduced an annualized run rate (ARR) revenue metric to track its commercial expansion as data center infrastructure comes online. Commercial execution now determines whether its contractual backing turns into actual cash flow. Three things management said on the call stand out.

The company's annualized run rate revenue, or projected yearly revenue based on active billing, will surge as 30 megawatts of data center power capacity enter active service. That operational activation converts initial infrastructure installations into cash-generating deployments under long-term agreements, with billing expected in January of 2027.

Rather than tapping high-cost corporate borrowing, management finances graphics processing unit (GPU) hardware using special purpose vehicles (SPVs), or isolated subsidiary companies created for specific infrastructure projects. These debt facilities lock in funding directly against customer agreements where clients must pay regardless of usage.

Customer pricing on multiyear agreements has increased as specialized compute capacity grows scarce across global markets. High contribution margins, or the proportion of revenue remaining after direct operating costs, allow project returns to pay back initial equipment costs well inside contract terms.

Customers are scrambling for immediate power and compute access, and management is not hiding its satisfaction about its secured data center footprint. The company holds pre-connected power infrastructure in Australia and an anchor partnership with NVIDIA, giving it clear advantages over rivals stuck in utility grid delay queues. Management keeps a close watch on cluster deployment timelines and debt execution.

Converting a total contract value of $9.6 billion into active billing remains the ultimate test for the business as it ramps hardware deployments into 2027.

#3007. Where Will Nvidia Stock Be in 20 Years? The Answer Might Surprise You.

Nvidia's future isn't as hard to forecast as you might think.

By Ryan Vanzo – Nov 22, 2026 at 12:00AM EST

Nvidia (NVDA -14.01%) stock is currently the cheapest it has been in over a decade. Shares trade at just 16 times trailing earnings. That's even cheaper than the company's previous decade-low valuation set in early 2019.

The company's shrinking valuation has little to do with its current financial situation. The GPU maker generated $43.8 billion in free cash flow last quarter. Sales growth this year is expected to approach 100% year over year, with another 71% growth expected the following year. Profits are expected to rise in tandem, causing shares to trade at less than 10 times forward earnings.

The macro environment for Nvidia is similarly bullish. Research from Apollo Global Management (APO -4.41%) says:

What, then, is dragging down Nvidia stock? There are three main culprits.

First, the company is dealing with the ongoing fallout of CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy. The company could face regulatory blowback, export restrictions, and weaker long-term leadership following Huang's exit.

Second, reporting suggests that Nvidia engaged in a form of circular financing, injecting cash into artificial intelligence (AI) start-ups to absorb excess GPU supply.

Third, investors are concerned about potential margin compression as both hyperscalers and other GPU producers invest aggressively to scale their own chip production.

But here's the thing: If you commit to a 20-year holding period, few of these current concerns will ultimately matter.

Normally, it is difficult to forecast a company's next couple of decades. Nvidia's situation is surprisingly straightforward. While the company's dominant market share in AI GPUs is driven by long-term planning and software ecosystem investment, sales growth is largely driven by industrywide demand. In other words, Nvidia is a high-quality boat in a tide that will rise for decades to come.

"Nvidia has a wide economic moat," asserts research from Morningstar. "[I]ts competitive advantages should allow it to sustain profitability for 20 years," as its products and software are "needed to enable the exponentially growing market around artificial intelligence."

How quickly is that AI market growing, and how long will it sustain those growth rates?

"A massive wave of data center construction will have implications through 2050," stresses research from PwC. "The AI infrastructure cycle underway will likely dwarf previous investment booms in areas like railways, electrification, or the internet."

In no scenario does PwC forecast data center spending to fall under $20 trillion by 2050.

"Across all three scenarios, capex rises significantly through 2050," the firm predicts. "Faster AI adoption pushes capex to about $50 trillion through 2050; a slower adoption path limits the cycle to roughly $20 trillion."

While former CEO Jensen Huang was critical in developing Nvidia's current chip lineup and CUDA developer ecosystem, Nvidia's long-term future now relies just as much on industry trends as company-specific development.

Similarly, while near-term regulatory pressure or export restrictions may slightly reduce sales growth, the long-term global growth outlook remains intact.

Margin compression over time, meanwhile, is almost a certainty. But trading at less than 10 times forward earnings, much of these pressures are arguably already priced in. Compounding double-digit annual sales growth -- which should persist over the next two decades -- should more than offset margin normalization, especially considering the next few years should still generate industry-leading profitability.

What will Nvidia be like 20 years from now? The company will almost certainly be much bigger than it is today. And given how cheaply the stock is priced, I'm fairly certain that patient shareholders will be pleased following a multi-decade holding period.

However, the vast universe of dividend stocks can make selection challenging. Tracking the ratings of top Wall Street analysts can help shortlist attractive dividend stocks, as their recommendations are backed by in-depth research.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

#3003. Walker Kessler's first three-pointer as a Laker sparks resurgent second half

Lakers coaches didn't know why Walker Kessler was standing in the corner. But when Collin Sexton flung the ball to the center standing behind the three-point arc on the Lakers' first possession of the fourth quarter, Kessler knew what he was going to do with it.

"I'm confident in that shot," Kessler said with a smirk.

The 7-foot-2 center's strong second half sparked the Lakers' gritty 106-104 win over the Sacramento Kings on Friday at Crypto.com Arena. After Lakers coach JJ Redick "lit [him] up" at halftime, Kessler responded by scoring nine of his 15 points and grabbing six of his seven total rebounds after the break and draining the unexpected long-distance shot that put the Lakers up by one early in the fourth quarter.

Redick said the play, with the Lakers (14-3) trailing by two to start the fourth quarter, was a little unorganized, leading to their center somehow standing in the corner. Kessler, who hadn't attempted a three all season and was 17 for 64 from three-point range during four seasons with the Utah Jazz, took instruction from Sexton to space to the corner instead of slash to the rim. Sexton whipped a one-handed pass over his head to Kessler, who methodically rose up over Dylan Cardwell's late closeout.

Redick told Kessler once during the preseason after a particular timeout that if the ball found him on a called play and it wasn't for a layup, the center should still shoot. Although Kessler has faith from the coaches and works on his jump shot, Redick isn't anointing the 25-year-old an official stretch five. His teammates don't mind.

"I mean, if he shoots it like that, I'll keep finding him," guard Quentin Grimes said with a laugh. "If he's going to keep cashing it all net, I want more of them. Keep shooting."

Read more: Quentin Grimes' late three-pointer lifts Lakers to narrow win over Kings

Kessler's go-ahead three-pointer highlighted the Lakers' comeback from an 11-point deficit with 11:25 remaining in the third. During a homestand that appeared to be favorable but has turned into a difficult slog, the Lakers have relied on unexpected characters to star in big moments.

Grimes hit back-to-back three-pointers in the fourth quarter against the Charlotte Hornets on Tuesday to fuel his career-high 47 points. The Lakers staged most of their 18-point comeback during the beginning of the fourth quarter when superstar Luka Doncic was on the bench. They trailed by 13 at the end of the third quarter. When Doncic subbed back in with 6:54 remaining, the Lakers, playing the majority of the stretch with two-way center Carson Cooper, were down by only four.

Cooper was playing the critical minutes because Kessler missed the game with lower right leg soreness. With Kessler back against the Kings (1-14), the Lakers repeated their fourth-quarter heroics, turning a two-point deficit after three quarters into a seven-point lead by the time Doncic returned.

Coaches made small rotational changes to the unit Friday, opting to start the fourth with Kessler, Sexton, Grimes, Matisse Thybulle and Jake LaRavia. Forward Sandro Mamukelashvili previously started the fourth quarter in recent games with Austin Reaves sidelined. Still feeling out the best lineups for the team, Redick said the exact groupings are "going to be a process."

The Lakers aren't fazed by the adjustments.

"I think we have a lot of heart and our ability to just make things work," said Thybulle, who had 14 points and four made three-pointers Friday. "We've been throwing out a whole bunch of different lineups. … Just being able to be adaptable, I think, has been a huge thing for everyone on the roster."

Lakers center Walker Kessler scores off an offensive rebound in the first half against the Sacramento Kings on Friday. (Gina Ferazzi / Los Angeles Times)

The Lakers are 6-1 in the last seven games in which Doncic or Reaves have missed time. The superstars have only played three quarters of a game together in the last seven games. Doncic missed the game at Detroit with lower back soreness, and Reaves, who was sick in Atlanta on Nov. 9, has missed the last four games with a left heel bruise. The Lakers hope to have him back by at least next Friday on the road against San Antonio.

Kessler was sidelined against Charlotte for the first time this season. Like the rest of his teammates, he struggled against the Utah Jazz on Wednesday, finishing with the quietest 10-point, 11-rebound double-double imaginable. He was in danger of fading into the background again against Sacramento before Redick jolted the team awake at halftime.

"I wasn't playing physical," Kessler said. "I wasn't going up to dunk the ball. I was missing some more touches around the rim. And then defensively, being undisciplined. Jumping at stuff I don't need to jump at. He definitely lit into me. It was good. I needed it. That's what makes a good coach. Knowing when guys need that and when guys don't."

While Redick said afterward he believed he was able to regulate his emotions during his halftime talk to the team, Doncic, who finished with 25 points and eight assists, characterized it more plainly.

"He yells," Doncic said. "But I'm used to it."

Kessler, a centerpiece for a franchise with championship expectations, is getting used to the demands of this new spotlight. He dazzled with 48 points in his first two games in which he made 22 of 26 shots, including 10 dunks in his perfect debut. But coaches demanded more production from his rebounding and fans are unrelenting in their calls for more.

"I know obviously you're on a bigger stage and stuff like that, but my teammates and coaching staff have done a really good job of picking everyone up even though we're struggling or we were struggling these past two games," Kessler said. "I'm not really focused too much on the outside but I understand that the L.A. fans expect a certain kind of performance. And I think it's not just making shots, but playing with effort and energy and I can completely respect that."

When Kessler goes to the bench, he hears jeers from fans imploring him to play harder.

When he hit that three from the corner, he heard some of the loudest cheers of the night.

#3002. Yelp: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Management is betting that a $250 million non-advertising revenue target can carry Yelp through a stalled local ad market before 2028.

By The Motley Fool Team – Nov 22, 2026 at 12:23AM EST

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 5, 2026, Yelp (YELP -1.99%) announced a 1% year-over-year decline in net revenue to $371 million as weak consumer demand weighed on core advertising. While local ad budgets remain under pressure, rapid growth in artificial intelligence (AI) tools and data licensing offers a new path to long-term value creation. Three things management said on the call stand out.

Core ad revenue fell across both services and restaurant categories due to cautious business spending. To offset that drag, management is leaning into data licensing with technology partners and subscription software products.

Restaurant operators and home service professionals are adopting automated voice technology to handle calls and convert customer leads. Yelp Host, the company's internal call-answering tool, expanded rapidly after integrating advanced conversational models.

Management reduced diluted shares outstanding by 15% year over year after buying back $200 million of stock in 2026. It paused the repurchase program in the third quarter to pay down its revolving credit facility before resuming in 2027.

Local advertising headwinds show no signs of immediate relief, with persistent inflation and high labor costs weighing on business ad budgets. Yelp relies on structural advantages like high-intent search traffic and deep partnerships with leading technology platforms to preserve engagement.

Management is watching key operating themes, including pricing discipline in paid project acquisition and cost control around stock-based compensation (SBC).

The broader strategy hinges on transforming search interactions into automated lead conversions across services and dining. Long-term returns depend on whether software revenue can outpace macro softness in local advertising.

#3000. The 2 ETFs I'd Buy Today: 1 for Growth, 1 for Dividends

One of these funds is down around 18% from its record while the other has risen. Why own both?

By Daniel Sparks – Nov 22, 2026 at 12:37AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Vanguard Morningstar Growth ETF ›

In the last seven weeks, two low-cost stock funds have moved in opposite directions.

The Vanguard Morningstar Growth ETF (VUG -5.32%) closed Oct. 6 at a record $92.64. As of this writing, it trades near $76, about 18% under that high. The Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF (SCHD -0.76%), meanwhile, is up about 3% since Oct. 6 and is within about 6% of its own record.

That split is a big reason I like owning these two funds together. The growth fund holds many of the fastest-growing large businesses in the U.S., while the dividend fund pays a yield over eight times the growth fund's. And when one has a rough patch, the other has tended to hold up better.

The growth fund tracks the Morningstar US Large Cap Growth Index, and it owned 135 stocks at the end of September. At the time, Nvidia, Apple, Microsoft, and Alphabet accounted for about 45% of the fund's assets.

Technology stocks make up about 69% of the fund by Vanguard's classification. But it's not just a tech fund. Its 10 biggest holdings also include Amazon and Tesla, and consumer discretionary stocks are around 13% of the portfolio.

What investors get for that concentration is growth. By Vanguard's measure, the fund's current stocks grew their earnings around 33% a year on average in the last five years, and the fund was valued at about 29 times earnings at the end of October. Its share price has dropped about 11% since then, so that valuation arguably looks more reasonable now. In the 10 years through Sept. 30, the fund returned around 18% a year. What's more, its 0.03% expense ratio means just $3 in yearly costs per $10,000 invested.

Sure, that sort of growth can come with bigger drops. The fund lost around 33% in 2022, counting dividends.

Its 30-day SEC yield (a standardized gauge of the income a fund earns) is also just 0.37%. Put another way, dividends don't do much to cushion a fall like the current one.

I wouldn't bet on a quick bounce. But I think 10 years is long enough for companies that have grown this fast to grow into their prices.

Schwab's fund tracks the Dow Jones U.S. Dividend 100 Index, which chooses dividend payers using financial ratios meant to point to the quality and sustainability of their payouts. It owned 102 stocks as of Nov. 19.

Its biggest holdings were Procter & Gamble, Texas Instruments, Coca-Cola, and Home Depot, all between around 4% and 5% of the fund. The mix looks almost nothing like the growth fund's. Consumer staples, healthcare, and energy stocks made up around 55% of the portfolio in Schwab's newest breakdown, but information technology was about 12%.

Income is the top reason to own it. Its 30-day SEC yield was 3.18% as of Nov. 18, and it costs 0.06% a year, or $6 per $10,000.

Schwab, meanwhile, put the fund's holdings at around 18.5 times earnings at the end of October, well under the growth fund's 29 times earnings (but the two companies might calculate the number a bit differently).

This fund won't keep up when growth stocks are running, though. It returned around 12% a year in the decade ending Sept. 30, versus about 18% for the growth fund. Its dividend growth has also cooled. The last four quarterly distributions total around $1.05 a share, only about 2% more than the four before them.

The two funds' best and worst years haven't matched up. In 2022, the growth fund fell around 33% but the dividend fund lost only about 3%, including dividends. The next year flipped that, with the growth fund returning about 47% in 2023 and the dividend fund about 5%. And since Oct. 6 this year, the growth fund has slid around 18% but the dividend fund has risen about 3%.

Someone dividing $10,000 equally between them would pay about $4.50 a year in fund costs and earn a combined yield of around 1.8%.

Over the next decade, I'd expect the growth fund to do most of the heavy lifting on returns, but likely not at its 18% yearly rate of the last decade. The dividend fund's job is to keep cash coming and hold up when growth stocks sell off, the way they have since October.

I'd consider buying both funds today. And with the growth fund around 18% off its record, it's the one I'd add to first.
